extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and creative practitioners (poets, writers, sculptors) interested in Greek myth, religion, and art-history
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical principles for representing the Demeter–Persephone myth in poetry, prose, ritual-description, and sculpture — covering narrative tone, ritual detail, iconography, and how artistic style shapes meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix ritual-symbolism with narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: The hymn-writer mingles symbolical imitations with the outlines of the original story; the dramatic person of the mysteries mixes itself with the primitive mythical figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When retelling Demeter's story, interweave ritual gestures, symbols, and ceremonial imagery with plot narration rather than treating ritual as mere background. This blending can increase impressiveness and link inner sense with outward ritual imagery; avoid a purely dispassionate, detached narration that strips ritual of its emotive force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent myth as gradual development
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of development, of degrees, of a slow and natural growth, impeded here, diverted there, is the illuminating thought which earlier critics lacked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat variations and later accretions (Orphic elements, civic rites, scenic elaborations) as part of the myth's organic evolution; avoid assuming a single 'original' authoritative version. Show how rituals, local cults, and poetic fashions shape the story over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the mystic silence of mysteries
rubrics_metrics.description: "No tongue may speak of them" — the prolonged, mystic silence is a defining quality of the mysteries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain an element of secrecy or withheld knowledge when portraying initiatory rites; the sense of something 'not to be spoken' contributes to aura. You may juxtapose secrecy with the public spectacle around it to heighten contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include public, sensory ritual spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Processions (torchlight, sacred basket, image of Iacchus), nocturns, libations, purifications, and the 'great night' are central ceremonial incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete sensory details (torches, incense, songs, torchlight processions, sea-bathing purifications, the sacred basket with poppy-seeds and pomegranates) to render religious observance vivid. Note that different spectators may interpret these spectacles differently — show variety of reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground myth in local topography and objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposition of sacred places — threshing-floor of Triptolemus, the rocky seat where Demeter rested, the well of Callichorus — links story and ritual to place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ specific locales and artefacts to anchor mythic action: stones, wells, threshing-floors, temple niches, votive lamps. Topographical detail can provide plausibility and symbolic resonance (e.g., caves for chthonic associations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small, homely touches to evoke pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: Ovid's treatment translates the story into homely circumstances (stone of sorrow, a poor man's cottage, a consoling little girl) to produce intimate pathos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humanizing minutiae — a poppy gathered, a child's question, a mother's kiss — can make divine sorrow immediate and moving. This approach suits elegiac or intimate tones; avoid over-idealizing grand ritual when aiming for domestic pathos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflect variant poetic styles and their effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Different poets (Homeric hymn, Callimachus, Theocritus, Euripides, Claudian, Ovid) cast the story in different registers: monumental, prosaic, pastoral, mystic-enthusiastic, pictorial, homely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a stylistic register appropriate to the interpretive aim: monumental for solemnity, pastoral for popular feeling, Orphic-mystic for ecstatic intensity, pictorial for sensory color, homely for intimacy. Be aware that style changes what aspects of the myth are emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict transformative identifications and Orphic influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Orphic influence Demeter is blended with Rhea Cybele; Dionysus Zagreus is introduced; the story adopts mystical and ecstatic elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When showing late or syncretic versions, incorporate cross-identifications and new motifs (mother-of-gods imagery, Bacchic cymbals, ecstatic motion). Make clear whether you are presenting an archaic, classical, or later syncretic form of the myth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve ambiguity of Persephone/Kore
rubrics_metrics.description: Kore is the goddess of summer and Persephone the goddess of death; she remains ambiguous — associated with flowers and fruit yet risen from the dead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with Persephone's dual nature — fertility and chthonic bride — to create emotional and symbolic complexity. Avoid flattening her into a single, unambiguous role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show both exalted/artistic and popular/folk religious elements
rubrics_metrics.description: High art humanises and refines religious conceptions, but votive figures, lead spells (katadesmoi), and provincial superstitions show a darker, popular side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance idealising artistic depictions with evidence of popular practice (binding spells, lamp-offerings, magic petitions). Including these elements prevents a sanitised, exclusively aesthetic account of belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sculptural vocabulary to express inner states
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculpture's function is to give visible aesthetic expression to the constituent parts of the ideal: seated Demeter, veiled, peplos folds, eyes looking upwards, hands of ivory, gold drapery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In visual or ekphrastic writing, translate internal emotion into posture, drapery, gaze, material (ivory, gold), and scale. For pathos, emphasize signs like a veiled, aged face, heavy parallel folds, an upward glance, or a slightly enlarged scale to convey monumentality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for stylistic school when designing figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Praxiteles' school: grace, Asiatic sinuosity and tenderness; Pheidias: severe ethical tension; later Roman poets/ornament: pictorial colour and tapestry-like description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If adopting a sculptural or painterly idiom, choose the 'school' to determine line, grace, and emotive emphasis. Praxitelean grace favors tenderness and relief; Pheidian treatment emphasizes ethical solemnity and monumentality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow multiple audience receptions and partial meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Various spectators may put many different senses, and how little definite meaning they may have even for those who officiate in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When showing ritual or public scenes, depict divergent understandings among participants and onlookers. Do not assume universal comprehension of symbolic acts — ambiguity and multiplicity of interpretation are authentic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include the grotesque or unhellenic as part of the tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: The myth had an unlovelier side — grotesque images like the Black Demeter with horse's head and reptiles; such forms remind us of earlier, rougher cultic expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not omit monstrous, archaic, or locally peculiar variants; their presence provides historical depth and prevents over-refinement. Use them deliberately to contrast with refined artistic ideals.
